original.stem: Plant lifecycles can be distinguished as annual, biennial and perennial.
original.questionText: Explain any two plant lifecycles and provide an example of each one.

rows.verbatim: First lifecycle explained — Annual: Completes its life cycle in one year
accepts: Biennial: Completes its life cycle in two years
Perennial: Flower and reproduce for multiple years

rows.verbatim: Example of the first lifecycle — wheat
accepts: carrot
perennial ryegrass
rows.contextNote: The example must match the lifecycle explained in the row above - the scheme pairs them line by line (annual/wheat, biennial/carrot, perennial/perennial ryegrass). Any other valid plant of the same lifecycle scores.

rows.verbatim: Second lifecycle explained — Biennial: Completes its life cycle in two years
accepts: Annual: Completes its life cycle in one year
Perennial: Flower and reproduce for multiple years

rows.verbatim: Example of the second lifecycle — carrot
accepts: wheat
perennial ryegrass
rows.contextNote: The example must match the lifecycle explained in the row above - the scheme pairs them line by line (annual/wheat, biennial/carrot, perennial/perennial ryegrass). Any other valid plant of the same lifecycle scores.

original.notes: The scheme prints three lifecycles at (3+2) each but the paper asks for any TWO, so the tariff is (3+2)+(3+2) = 10, not 15. Rows 1-2 are whichever lifecycle the student explained first and rows 3-4 the second; annual and biennial are the worked pair and the perennial wording sits in accepts on both explanation rows. Examples are openList because the scheme adds '(Any other valid example of a plant)', and each example row carries a contextNote so a student cannot claim an example belonging to a different lifecycle.

original.stem: Question 14, part (b). The question is set on soil compaction: the paper has already shown crop growth in compacted and uncompacted soil and a graph of water availability by soil type. Part (b) turns to an investigation you carry out yourself, so the labelled diagram is one you draw, not one printed on the paper.
original.questionText: Compare, with the aid of a labelled diagram, the capillarity of a compacted and uncompacted soil. State the results of this investigation.

rows.verbatim: Put cotton wool or muslin cloth in open end of one tube (and place in retort stand)
obtain dry soil sample
rows.contextNote: The scheme's step reads in full 'obtain dry soil sample and compact one half of the sample' — compacting one half is the point of the comparison.

rows.verbatim: place equal amounts of compacted soil in open end of the tubes and uncompacted soil in the other open-ended tube
place both tubes in equal amounts of water
measure or observe the level of water in each tube
rows.contextNote: The scheme's pool also carries 'leave for a suitable valid time' and closes with 'other valid method', so a sound step of your own that is not printed here still scores.

original.notes: The paper prints 17 for this part: 4x4 for the method plus one mark for stating the result. The result entry reads '*Result: valid result for investigation described' — a tariff with no answer in it, which cannot be a row, so the card covers the 16 method marks and totalMarks is 16 rather than 17. Reviewer should note that gap. bestNofParts because the scheme lists more steps than the four that score. Row 2 stops at 'obtain dry soil sample' because the 4x4 mark cell is typeset inside that step in the extracted markdown; the full step is in its contextNote. 'leave for a suitable valid time' is left out of the rows as a time instruction rather than an answer.
